newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's king says Berisha agrees to referendum.
newsitem.headline: Albania's king says Berisha agrees to referendum.

text.p: Albania's King Leka I said on Friday that President Sali Berisha had agreed to hold a referendum on whether to restore the monarchy 58 years after his father fled the country.

Leka, who was two days old when he first went into exile, said after the historic meeting with Berisha on Friday that the president was now willing to allow Albanians to vote on the issue. But he said political parties and Berisha would still have to determine the timing of a referendum.

"The meeting was warm and friendly," Leka said in an interview with Reuters. "He said the referendum would be on the agenda and would be carried out. But it would be up to the political partners and himself as to when that would happen."
Berisha's government unceremoniously tossed Leka out of the country in 1993 within hours of his first visit because authorities said his passport, marked "Kingdom of Albania", was invalid.
Leka returned from exile a second time last week carrying the same passport. This time he received a triumphant welcome from Albanians as he drove into Tirana from the airport.

"It is very difficult to express the emotions I felt," Leka said in the interview at a luxurious guest house belonging to his royalist Legality Movement party. "It is wonderful to be back here. It is wonderful to see my people."
Leka said the restoration of the monarchy could help unify the country, shattered by months of violence following the collapse of dubious investment schemes.
About 300 people have been killed and more than 700 injured in the armed anarchy that has plagued the country.
Leka's father King Zog fled with his family in 1939 before invading Italian fascist forces.
"The situation that has been created in the country needs a stabilising factor and I think in me they see a stabilising factor," he said.

"There is not one big problem. It is a thousand big problems that have to be addressed," he said. "I think it is primarily a question of bringing back politicial stability, peace and unity. I see myself being a factor in trying to achieve that."
Leka has been living with his Australian-born wife and 15-year-old son in South Africa. At 2.05 metres (six feet eight inches), he dwarfs most of his countrymen.
He said he felt he was still the legal leader of Albania based on a constitution adopted in 1928.
"The issue is whether the people will ratify the constitution or vote for a republic, in which case I will become a private citizen," he said.
Asked whether he would stay in Albania if the referendum fails, he replied: "Why not? It's my country."
